title: Separation of Powers
body: In The Spirit of the Laws (1748), Montesquieu argued that legislative, executive and judicial power should be held by different bodies. The idea strongly shaped the United States Constitution and modern democracies.

title: Women's Suffrage
body: In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the vote in national elections. Most Western countries followed in the first half of the 20th century, often after long campaigns by the suffrage movement.

title: The United Nations
body: The UN Charter was signed in San Francisco in June 1945 and the organisation formally came into being that autumn. The five permanent members of the Security Council hold a veto: the United States, Russia, China, the United Kingdom and France.

title: The Freedom of the Press Act of 1766
body: Sweden's 1766 act is regarded as the world's first constitutional protection of press freedom. It also introduced an early form of the principle of public access to official documents.

title: The European Union
body: The Treaty of Rome of 1957 created the European Economic Community. The Maastricht Treaty of 1992 founded the European Union and laid the ground for the single currency.

title: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
body: The UN General Assembly adopted the declaration on 10 December 1948. The drafting commission was chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt. It is not binding in itself but has inspired a series of binding human rights treaties.

title: Athenian Democracy
body: Reforms by Cleisthenes around 508 BC gave Athens a system in which citizens voted directly on laws in the assembly. Only adult male citizens took part, excluding women, slaves and foreigners, but it is the best-known early democracy.

title: The United States Constitution
body: Drafted in Philadelphia in 1787, it is one of the oldest written national constitutions still in force. It divides power between three branches and between federal and state governments. The first ten amendments, the Bill of Rights, were added in 1791.

title: NATO
body: The North Atlantic Treaty Organization was founded in 1949 as a Western defence alliance. Its core is Article 5: an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.

title: The Rule of Law
body: The rule of law means that everyone, including those in power, is subject to laws that are public, clear and applied equally by independent courts. It is distinct from 'rule by law', where law is merely a tool of those in power.

title: The Westminster System
body: Named after the British Parliament, this system makes the government depend on the confidence of an elected parliament. The prime minister and cabinet sit in parliament and can be removed by it. It has been adopted in many former British colonies.

title: The Geneva Conventions
body: The first Geneva Convention of 1864 protected wounded soldiers. The four conventions of 1949 extend protection to the sick, shipwrecked, prisoners of war and civilians, and form the core of international humanitarian law.

title: Duverger's Law
body: Political scientist Maurice Duverger observed that first-past-the-post voting tends to produce two dominant parties, while proportional representation favours many parties. It is a tendency rather than a strict law, but it helps explain differences between party systems.

title: The Beveridge Report
body: William Beveridge's 1942 report proposed a comprehensive system of social insurance in Britain to fight 'want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness'. It laid the ground for the post-war British welfare state, including the National Health Service.

title: What Makes a State
body: The Montevideo Convention of 1933 sets out four widely cited criteria for statehood: a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to enter into relations with other states. Recognition by other states is a separate question.

title: The European Convention on Human Rights
body: Signed in Rome in 1950 by members of the Council of Europe, the convention protects civil and political rights such as the right to life, a fair trial and freedom of expression. Its distinctive feature is the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, to which individuals can bring cases against states. It is separate from the European Union.

title: The Gadaa System
body: Gadaa is the traditional system of self-government of the Oromo people of Ethiopia and Kenya, organising men into generation grades that pass through successive stages of eight years each. Leaders are elected for a single eight-year term and power passes peacefully from one group to the next. UNESCO inscribed it as intangible cultural heritage in 2016.

title: Pancasila
body: Proclaimed by Sukarno in 1945, Pancasila ('five principles') is the founding philosophy of the Indonesian state: belief in one God, a just and civilised humanity, the unity of Indonesia, democracy guided by deliberation, and social justice. Its broad monotheism was designed to unite a religiously diverse nation without making it an Islamic state.

title: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
body: In this 1792 book Mary Wollstonecraft argued that women seem inferior only because they are denied a proper education, and that they should be educated as rational beings and equal companions to men. Written in response to the revolutionary debates on rights in France and Britain, it is regarded as a founding text of liberal feminism.

title: Brazil's Golden Law
body: Signed by Princess Isabel on 13 May 1888, the Lei Áurea abolished slavery in Brazil without compensation to slave owners. Brazil had received more enslaved Africans than any other country in the Americas and was the last nation in the Western Hemisphere to end slavery. The monarchy fell the following year, partly because it had lost the support of landowners.

title: Justinian's Code
body: In the 520s and 530s the Byzantine emperor Justinian I had centuries of Roman law collected and systematised in what later became known as the Corpus Juris Civilis. Rediscovered in Western Europe around 1100 and studied at Bologna, it became the basis of the civil law tradition used across continental Europe, Latin America and beyond.

title: The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo
body: From 1977 mothers whose children had been 'disappeared' by Argentina's military dictatorship marched each week in front of the presidential palace in Buenos Aires, wearing white headscarves. Their protest defied a regime that banned public gatherings and drew world attention to state terror. Related groups later worked to trace children taken from detained parents.

title: The English Bill of Rights
body: Passed in 1689 after the Glorious Revolution placed William III and Mary II on the throne, the Bill of Rights barred the Crown from suspending laws, levying taxes or keeping a standing army in peacetime without Parliament's consent. It also protected free elections and freedom of speech in Parliament. It is a cornerstone of constitutional monarchy and influenced the American Bill of Rights.

title: Nepal's Abolition of the Monarchy
body: After a decade-long Maoist insurgency and mass protests in 2006, Nepal's newly elected Constituent Assembly abolished the centuries-old Shah monarchy in May 2008 and declared a federal democratic republic. After years of deadlock, a new constitution was adopted in 2015.

title: From the OAU to the African Union
body: The Organisation of African Unity was founded in Addis Ababa in 1963 to support decolonisation and defend the sovereignty of new states, but its principle of non-interference kept it largely silent on abuses within them. It was replaced in 2002 by the African Union, whose founding act allows intervention in a member state in cases of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.

title: The Mandate of Heaven
body: The Zhou dynasty, which overthrew the Shang in the 11th century BC, justified its rule by claiming that Heaven grants the right to rule to a virtuous ruler and withdraws it from a corrupt one. Natural disasters and revolts could be read as signs that the mandate had been lost. The idea legitimised both imperial rule and successful rebellion throughout Chinese history.

title: UN Peacekeeping
body: The first UN military observer mission was sent to the Middle East in 1948, and the first armed peacekeeping force was deployed in 1956 during the Suez Crisis. Blue-helmeted peacekeepers, contributed by member states and lightly armed, monitor ceasefires and help carry out peace agreements, normally with the consent of the parties. UN peacekeeping forces received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1988.

title: Ibn Khaldun's Asabiyyah
body: In the Muqaddimah (1377), the North African scholar Ibn Khaldun argued that dynasties rise on asabiyyah, the group solidarity of hardy, often nomadic peoples, and decline as luxury erodes it, typically within a few generations. His cyclical theory of how states form and fall has earned him a place among the forerunners of sociology and political science.

title: The American Civil Rights Movement
body: Through boycotts, sit-ins and marches, including the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955–56 sparked by Rosa Parks and the 1963 March on Washington, African Americans challenged segregation and disenfranchisement in the South. Led by figures such as Martin Luther King Jr., the movement won the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

title: The Cyrus Cylinder
body: This clay cylinder, inscribed in Akkadian after Cyrus the Great of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC, describes how he restored temples and allowed displaced peoples to return home. It is sometimes called the first charter of human rights, but most historians regard that label as anachronistic, since the text follows a traditional Mesopotamian genre of royal propaganda.

title: The May Fourth Movement
body: On 4 May 1919 students in Beijing protested against the Paris Peace Conference's decision to transfer Germany's rights in Shandong to Japan rather than return them to China. The protests grew into a broad cultural and political movement championing science, democracy and writing in vernacular Chinese. Its activists included several founders of the Chinese Communist Party, established in 1921.

title: Tocqueville's Democracy in America
body: After travelling through the United States in 1831–32, the French aristocrat Alexis de Tocqueville published Democracy in America in two volumes, in 1835 and 1840. He admired Americans' local self-government and voluntary associations, but warned of the 'tyranny of the majority' and of a soft despotism of conformity. It is a classic analysis of democratic society.

title: The Law of the Sea Convention
body: Concluded in 1982 after nearly a decade of negotiation, the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea sets the legal framework for the world's oceans. It fixes territorial waters at up to 12 nautical miles and gives coastal states exclusive economic zones of up to 200 nautical miles, while treating the deep seabed beyond national jurisdiction as the common heritage of mankind.

title: The Meiji Constitution
body: Promulgated in 1889, the Constitution of the Empire of Japan was the first modern constitution in East Asia. Modelled largely on Prussia's, it created an elected lower house in a parliament called the Diet but kept sovereignty with the emperor and gave the armed forces direct access to him. That weak civilian control is often seen as helping militarists dominate government in the 1930s.

title: The Constitution of Carthage
body: The Phoenician city of Carthage in North Africa was governed by two annually elected chief magistrates called suffetes, a council of elders, a court of 104 judges that held generals to account, and a popular assembly. Aristotle discussed it in his Politics alongside Sparta and Crete and praised it as a well-balanced constitution. It is one of the few non-Greek constitutions described in classical political thought.

title: The Nuremberg Trials
body: In 1945–46 an International Military Tribunal set up by the four main Allied powers tried leading Nazis for crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity. It established that individuals, including heads of state and officials acting on orders, can be held criminally responsible under international law. Its principles laid the foundation for later international criminal courts.

title: Rwanda's Gacaca Courts
body: After the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi, Rwanda's ordinary courts could not cope with more than 100,000 detained suspects. From the early 2000s until 2012 the country revived gacaca, a traditional form of community justice, with locally elected lay judges hearing well over a million cases. The courts were praised for speed and local participation but criticised for lacking fair-trial guarantees.

title: Kemalism
body: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, who founded the Republic of Turkey in 1923, pursued a programme later summed up in six principles: republicanism, nationalism, populism, statism, secularism and reformism. His government abolished the caliphate in 1924, replaced Islamic law with codes based on European models and introduced the Latin alphabet in 1928.

title: The Paris Agreement
body: Adopted in December 2015 by nearly every country in the world, the agreement aims to keep global warming well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C. Instead of imposing binding emission quotas, it asks each country to set its own nationally determined contributions, to be updated and strengthened every five years.

title: The Bandung Conference
body: In April 1955 leaders of 29 Asian and African countries, many newly independent, met in Bandung, Indonesia. Hosted by Sukarno and attended by figures such as Nehru, Zhou Enlai and Nasser, the conference condemned colonialism and called for cooperation among developing nations. It paved the way for the Non-Aligned Movement, founded in Belgrade in 1961.

title: The Secret Ballot
body: In 1856 the Australian colonies of Victoria and South Australia introduced government-printed ballot papers marked in private, which is why the secret ballot was long known as the 'Australian ballot'. Before it, voting was often public, leaving voters open to bribery and intimidation. Britain adopted it in 1872 and the method spread across the democratic world.

title: Simon de Montfort's Parliament
body: In 1265, while ruling England after capturing Henry III, the baron Simon de Montfort summoned a parliament that included not only nobles and clergy but also knights from each county and burgesses from the towns. It is seen as a milestone in the development of the House of Commons. Edward I's 'Model Parliament' of 1295 made such representation more regular.

title: The Mabo Decision
body: In 1992 the High Court of Australia ruled in favour of Eddie Mabo and other Meriam people of the Torres Strait, rejecting the doctrine that Australia had been terra nullius, land belonging to no one, when the British arrived. It recognised that native title to land could survive colonisation. Parliament responded with the Native Title Act of 1993.

title: The Manden Charter
body: According to oral tradition, the Manden Charter was proclaimed at Kurukan Fuga when the Mali Empire was founded under Sundiata Keita in the 13th century. Passed down by griots, it sets out principles such as respect for human life, social harmony and the rejection of enslavement by raiding. Its date and original content cannot be verified, but UNESCO recognised it as intangible cultural heritage in 2009.

title: Burke and Modern Conservatism
body: In Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790), the Irish-born statesman Edmund Burke attacked the attempt to rebuild society from abstract principles. He defended tradition, gradual reform and inherited institutions as the accumulated wisdom of generations, and predicted that the Revolution would end in violence. The book is widely regarded as a founding text of modern conservatism.

title: Federalism
body: In a federal system, power is constitutionally divided between a central government and regional units such as states or provinces, each with an area of authority protected by the constitution. Examples include the United States, Switzerland, India and Nigeria. Federalism can accommodate regional and ethnic diversity, but produces recurring disputes over which level decides what.

title: Arendt and Totalitarianism
body: In The Origins of Totalitarianism (1951), Hannah Arendt argued that Nazism and Stalinism were a new form of government that used ideology and terror to dominate every aspect of life and to isolate individuals. Unlike older tyrannies, it sought total control rather than mere obedience. Her later report on the trial of Adolf Eichmann coined the phrase 'the banality of evil'.

title: The Ottoman Millet System
body: The Ottoman Empire allowed recognised religious communities, such as Greek Orthodox Christians, Armenians and Jews, to run their own family law, education and charity under their own religious leaders. Historians debate how formal this 'millet' system was before it was codified in the 19th century. It is a classic example of autonomy for minorities that is based on community rather than territory.

title: Aristotle's Politics
body: In the Politics, Aristotle classified constitutions by whether one, a few or many rule, and whether they rule for the common good (kingship, aristocracy, polity) or for themselves (tyranny, oligarchy, democracy). He called humans political animals who can flourish only in a community. His comparison of many Greek city constitutions makes him a founder of political science.

title: Pan-Africanism
body: Pan-Africanism holds that Africans and people of African descent share common interests and should unite. Shaped by figures such as W. E. B. Du Bois and Marcus Garvey and by a series of Pan-African Congresses from 1919, it inspired independence leaders including Kwame Nkrumah, who led Ghana to independence in 1957.

title: The Tanzimat Reforms
body: Between 1839 and 1876 the Ottoman Empire carried out the Tanzimat ('reorganisation'), modernising its army, law, education and administration. Imperial edicts of 1839 and 1856 promised security of life and property and equality for all subjects regardless of religion. The era culminated in the first Ottoman constitution of 1876, which was suspended two years later.

title: The League of Nations
body: Created by the peace settlement after the First World War and founded in 1920 with its seat in Geneva, the League was the first worldwide organisation of states dedicated to keeping the peace through collective security. The United States never joined, and the League failed to stop aggression by Japan, Italy and Germany in the 1930s. It was dissolved in 1946 and succeeded by the United Nations.

title: Mill's Harm Principle
body: In On Liberty (1859), John Stuart Mill argued that the only legitimate reason for exercising power over anyone against their will is to prevent harm to others; a person's own good is not enough. He defended free speech on the grounds that suppressed opinions may be true, and warned against society's pressure to conform as well as against state power.

title: The Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist
body: In lectures given in 1970, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini argued that in the absence of the hidden Imam a qualified Shia jurist should hold political authority. After the 1979 revolution this doctrine of velayat-e faqih was written into the constitution of the Islamic Republic of Iran, which places a Supreme Leader above elected institutions. Many senior Shia clerics have rejected the doctrine.

title: Rome's Mixed Constitution
body: From about 509 BC the Roman Republic was governed by two annually elected consuls, a Senate of former magistrates and popular assemblies, while tribunes could veto acts against the plebeians. The Greek historian Polybius praised it as a mixed constitution combining monarchy, aristocracy and democracy. The model inspired the American founders and the idea of checks and balances.

title: Self-Determination of Peoples
body: The principle that peoples have the right freely to choose their political status gained force after the First World War, championed in different ways by Woodrow Wilson and Lenin. It was written into the UN Charter and the 1966 human rights covenants. Its tension with the territorial integrity of existing states is one of the hardest problems of international law.

title: The Declaration of Independence
body: Adopted by the Continental Congress on 4 July 1776 and drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson, it announced the separation of thirteen American colonies from Britain. Its preamble holds that all men are created equal, with unalienable rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, and that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed.

title: The Althing
body: Founded in 930, Iceland's Althing was an open-air assembly at Thingvellir where chieftains met each summer to make laws and settle disputes, while a lawspeaker recited the law from memory. Though abolished in 1800 and restored in 1845, it is often called one of the oldest parliaments in the world, and its name lives on in Iceland's national parliament.

title: The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation
body: Founded in Shanghai in 2001 by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, the organisation grew out of earlier border agreements between China and its post-Soviet neighbours. It focuses on regional security, against what its members call terrorism, separatism and extremism, as well as economic cooperation. India and Pakistan joined in 2017.

title: South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission
body: Set up in 1995 and chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, the commission heard testimony from victims and perpetrators of human rights violations under apartheid. Perpetrators who fully disclosed politically motivated crimes could be granted amnesty. It became an influential, and much debated, model of transitional justice for other countries emerging from conflict or dictatorship.

title: The Communist Manifesto
body: Written by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels and published in London in February 1848, it opens its argument with the claim that the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles. It predicted that the proletariat would overthrow the bourgeoisie and abolish private property, and ended with the call for workers of all countries to unite.

title: The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty
body: Opened for signature in 1968 and in force from 1970, the treaty recognises as nuclear-weapon states the five that had tested a weapon before 1967, and commits other parties not to acquire them. In return, the nuclear states undertake to pursue disarmament, and all parties may use nuclear energy peacefully under safeguards of the International Atomic Energy Agency.

title: The Gana-Sanghas of Ancient India
body: Around the time of the Buddha, northern India contained not only kingdoms but also gana-sanghas, states governed by assemblies of a ruling clan, such as the Vajji confederacy centred on Vaishali and the Shakyas. Buddhist texts describe their assemblies meeting to debate and decide matters. They are sometimes called early republics, though power lay with a warrior aristocracy, and most were absorbed by expanding kingdoms such as Magadha.

title: Nationalism
body: Nationalism holds that the nation, a people bound by shared culture, language or history, should govern itself in its own state. It spread with the American and French Revolutions, reshaped 19th-century Europe and later powered anti-colonial movements in Asia and Africa. Scholars such as Benedict Anderson, who called nations 'imagined communities', see them as largely modern, though others stress older roots.

title: Grotius and the Law of Nations
body: The Dutch jurist Hugo Grotius argued in Mare Liberum (1609) that the seas are open to all nations, and in On the Law of War and Peace (1625) that natural law binds states even in wartime. Writing during the Thirty Years' War, he set out rules on just causes for war and on conduct within it. He is often called a father of international law.

title: The Mongol Kurultai
body: Among the Mongols and other steppe peoples, a kurultai was a great assembly of princes and chiefs that chose the khan and decided on war. A kurultai proclaimed Temüjin as Genghis Khan in 1206, and after his death new great khans had to be confirmed in the same way. Succession disputes that kurultais failed to settle helped split the Mongol Empire.

title: The Responsibility to Protect
body: Endorsed by world leaders at the UN World Summit in 2005, the Responsibility to Protect holds that every state must protect its population from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity. If a state manifestly fails to do so, the international community should act, using force only through the Security Council. It was a response to the failures in Rwanda and Srebrenica.

title: Weber's Three Types of Authority
body: The German sociologist Max Weber distinguished three sources of legitimate rule: traditional authority based on custom, charismatic authority based on a leader's extraordinary qualities, and legal-rational authority based on impersonal rules and bureaucracy. In 'Politics as a Vocation' (1919) he defined the state as a community that claims a monopoly on the legitimate use of physical force within a territory.

title: Marbury v. Madison
body: In this 1803 case the US Supreme Court, under Chief Justice John Marshall, held for the first time that it could strike down an Act of Congress that conflicted with the Constitution. The principle of judicial review became central to American government and has been adopted, in various forms, by constitutional courts around the world.

title: Gandhi's Satyagraha
body: Developed by Mohandas Gandhi in South Africa from 1906 and later in India, satyagraha ('holding firmly to truth') is a method of nonviolent resistance that seeks to convert opponents through self-suffering rather than to coerce them. Its best-known campaign was the Salt March of 1930. It inspired later movements worldwide, including the American civil rights movement.

title: The Treaty of Waitangi
body: Signed in 1840 by representatives of the British Crown and many Māori chiefs, the treaty is regarded as New Zealand's founding document. Its English and Māori versions differ significantly, notably on whether the chiefs ceded sovereignty or only a right of governance. Since 1975 the Waitangi Tribunal has investigated breaches of the treaty, leading to settlements with many iwi.

title: Fascism
body: Benito Mussolini founded the Fascist movement in Italy in 1919 and came to power after the March on Rome in 1922. Fascism glorified the nation and the leader, rejected both liberal democracy and Marxism, and used violence and mass mobilisation to build a one-party state; Nazi Germany drew on the same model. Scholars still debate how precisely to define it.

title: South Korea's Candlelight Protests
body: From late 2016 weekly candlelit demonstrations, drawing huge crowds over several months, demanded the removal of President Park Geun-hye over a corruption and influence-peddling scandal. The National Assembly impeached her in December 2016 and the Constitutional Court upheld the decision in March 2017, making her the first South Korean president removed from office through impeachment.

title: The Monroe Doctrine
body: In 1823 US President James Monroe declared that the Americas were closed to further European colonisation and that the United States would regard European intervention in the hemisphere as an unfriendly act. Little enforceable at first, it was later used to justify repeated US intervention in Latin America, notably through the Roosevelt Corollary of 1904.

title: Japan's Pacifist Constitution
body: Drafted under American occupation and taking effect in 1947, Japan's postwar constitution made the emperor a symbol of the state without governing powers. Its Article 9 renounces war as a sovereign right of the nation and the threat or use of force to settle international disputes. How this fits with Japan's Self-Defense Forces has been debated ever since.

title: The Indian National Congress
body: Founded in Bombay in 1885 as a forum for educated Indians seeking a greater share in government, the Congress became the main vehicle of the independence movement under leaders such as Gandhi and Nehru. It mobilised millions in non-cooperation and civil disobedience campaigns, and after independence in 1947 it governed India for most of its first decades.

title: The Twelve Tables
body: Around 450 BC the Roman Republic set down its laws on twelve tablets displayed in the Forum, partly in response to plebeians who complained that unwritten law favoured the patricians. The tablets themselves are lost and survive only in quotations by later authors. They stand at the start of Roman law, which later shaped the legal systems of much of Europe.

title: China's Imperial Examinations
body: Introduced under the Sui dynasty around 600 and expanded under the Tang and Song, the examinations selected state officials by testing their knowledge of the Confucian classics. In principle open to most men regardless of birth, they created a scholar-official class and lasted until 1905. The system was copied in Korea and Vietnam and is often said to have influenced European civil service exams.

title: Participatory Budgeting
body: In 1989 the Brazilian city of Porto Alegre began letting residents decide, through neighbourhood assemblies, how part of the municipal investment budget would be spent. The experiment was credited with shifting spending towards poorer districts and reducing clientelism. Participatory budgeting has since been adopted in various forms by many cities around the world.

title: The Sustainable Development Goals
body: Adopted by all UN member states in 2015, the 17 Sustainable Development Goals set targets for 2030, including ending extreme poverty and hunger, achieving gender equality and tackling climate change. They succeeded the eight Millennium Development Goals of 2000 and, unlike them, apply to rich as well as poor countries.

title: Al-Farabi's Virtuous City
body: The 10th-century philosopher al-Farabi, active in Baghdad and Damascus, wrote The Opinions of the People of the Virtuous City, adapting Plato's Republic to an Islamic setting. He argued that the best city is ruled by a philosopher-prophet who leads citizens to happiness, and analysed the ignorant and corrupt cities that fall short. He was known as the 'Second Teacher' after Aristotle.

title: The Genocide Convention
body: The word 'genocide' was coined in 1944 by the Polish-Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin. The UN General Assembly adopted the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide on 9 December 1948, the day before the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It defines genocide as acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.

title: The Oyo Mesi
body: In the Yoruba Oyo Empire, in what is now south-western Nigeria and Benin, the king or Alaafin was checked by the Oyo Mesi, a council of seven nobles. According to tradition, if the council lost confidence in the Alaafin it could signal that he must take his own life. The arrangement is often cited as an African example of institutional checks on royal power.

title: Germany's Basic Law
body: Adopted in 1949 for West Germany and extended to the whole country at reunification in 1990, the Basic Law was designed to prevent a repeat of the Weimar Republic's collapse. It declares human dignity inviolable, shields core principles from amendment, allows parties hostile to democracy to be banned, and lets parliament remove a chancellor only by electing a successor.

title: Populism
body: Populism is commonly defined as politics that divides society into a virtuous 'people' and a corrupt 'elite', and claims to speak for the people's will. It can be combined with left- or right-wing ideas, as in the American People's Party of the 1890s or Juan Perón's Argentina. Scholars disagree about whether it is best understood as an ideology, a style or a strategy.

title: The Iranian Constitutional Revolution
body: Between 1905 and 1911 protests by merchants, clerics and intellectuals forced the Qajar shah to grant a constitution and an elected parliament, the Majlis, in 1906. It was one of the first constitutional revolutions in Asia. Though weakened by internal conflict and by Russian and British intervention, it rooted the idea of constitutional government in Iran.

title: The Napoleonic Code
body: France's Civil Code of 1804, promoted by Napoleon, replaced a patchwork of regional customs with a single, clearly written law on persons, property and contracts. It enshrined equality before the law and secular authority, while strengthening the power of husbands and fathers. Spread by conquest and imitation, it shaped civil law in much of Europe, Latin America and the Middle East.

title: The Haudenosaunee Great Law of Peace
body: The Haudenosaunee or Iroquois Confederacy united five nations, later six, in what is now the north-eastern United States under an oral constitution known as the Great Law of Peace. Clan mothers chose the chiefs who sat in the common council and could remove them. The confederacy's founding date is disputed, as is the extent of its influence on the framers of the US Constitution.

title: The Constitution of India
body: Drafted by a Constituent Assembly whose drafting committee was chaired by B. R. Ambedkar, it came into force on 26 January 1950, which India celebrates as Republic Day. One of the longest written national constitutions, it created a federal parliamentary republic, granted universal adult suffrage from the outset and abolished untouchability.

title: Machiavelli's The Prince
body: Written around 1513 and published in 1532, Niccolò Machiavelli's The Prince advised rulers to judge actions by their results for the state rather than by conventional morality, arguing that it is safer to be feared than loved if one cannot be both. It made 'Machiavellian' a byword for cunning, though his Discourses on Livy reveal a committed republican.

title: The Refugee Convention
body: The 1951 UN Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees defines a refugee as a person outside their country with a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion. Its core principle, non-refoulement, forbids returning refugees to places where they face serious threats. A 1967 protocol removed its original limits in time and geography.

title: The Legalisation of Same-Sex Marriage
body: In 2001 the Netherlands became the first country to open civil marriage to same-sex couples, after Denmark had pioneered registered partnerships in 1989. Many countries followed through legislation, referendums such as Ireland's in 2015, or court rulings such as the US Supreme Court's decision in Obergefell v. Hodges in the same year. The change marked a rapid shift in law and public attitudes towards gay and lesbian people.

title: The International Criminal Court
body: Created by the Rome Statute of 1998, the court began work in The Hague in 2002 as the first permanent international court able to try individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, with the crime of aggression added later. Under the principle of complementarity it acts only when national courts are unwilling or unable to prosecute.

title: Bolívar's Jamaica Letter
body: Written in exile in Kingston in 1815, Simón Bolívar's letter explained the causes of Spanish America's struggle for independence and predicted the future of the new nations. He hoped for strong republics and even imagined a union of American states, but doubted that federalism and full democracy suited them at once. It is a key document of Latin American political thought.

title: Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles of the People
body: Sun Yat-sen, leader of the movement that overthrew the Qing dynasty in 1911–12, set out three principles: nationalism, democracy (or people's rights) and the people's livelihood. They became the official ideology of the Kuomintang and are named as the foundation of the Republic of China in its 1947 constitution. Sun is honoured as a founding father in both mainland China and Taiwan.

title: The Edict of Caracalla
body: In 212 AD the emperor Caracalla granted Roman citizenship to almost all free inhabitants of the empire, in a decree known as the Constitutio Antoniniana. The historian Cassius Dio claimed its real aim was to widen the tax base. It completed a centuries-long extension of citizenship from the city of Rome to Italy and the provinces, and brought most of the empire's people under Roman law.

title: The Organization of American States
body: Founded at a conference in Bogotá in 1948, the Organization of American States brings together the countries of the Americas to promote peace, democracy and cooperation. The same conference adopted the American Declaration of the Rights and Duties of Man, months before the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Its human rights system later grew to include an Inter-American Commission and an Inter-American Court of Human Rights.

title: The Declaration of the Rights of Man
body: Adopted by France's National Constituent Assembly in August 1789, it proclaimed that men are born and remain free and equal in rights, naming liberty, property, security and resistance to oppression as natural rights. It established national sovereignty and equality before the law. In 1791 Olympe de Gouges answered it with a Declaration of the Rights of Woman.

title: ASEAN
body: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations was founded in Bangkok in 1967 by Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand, and later expanded to take in the rest of Southeast Asia, with Timor-Leste becoming its 11th member in 2025. Its 'ASEAN way' stresses consensus and non-interference in members' internal affairs, which supporters credit with keeping regional peace and critics blame for weak action.

title: Japan's Alternate Attendance System
body: Under the Tokugawa shogunate, the system of sankin-kōtai, formalised in the 1630s, required regional lords (daimyo) to spend alternate years in the capital Edo and to leave their families there permanently. The cost of travel and two households drained their wealth and limited their capacity to rebel. It also stimulated roads, towns and trade during more than two centuries of peace.

title: The UN Declaration on Decolonisation
body: In December 1960 the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 1514, declaring that colonialism should be brought to a speedy and unconditional end and that subjection of peoples to alien domination is a denial of fundamental human rights. Passed as dozens of colonies were gaining independence, it guided the UN's work in dismantling the remaining colonial empires.

title: The Zhou Fengjian System
body: After overthrowing the Shang in the 11th century BC, the Zhou kings granted lands to relatives and allies as hereditary states, bound to the royal house by kinship, ritual and military duties. As royal power weakened, especially after the western capital was sacked in 771 BC and the court moved east, these states became effectively independent rivals. The system is often compared with European feudalism, though many historians warn against the analogy.

title: Akbar's Mansabdari System
body: The Mughal emperor Akbar, who reigned from 1556 to 1605, ranked nobles and officials by a numerical grade, or mansab, which fixed their status, pay and the number of cavalry they had to maintain. Ranks were generally not hereditary and were often paid through revenue assignments called jagirs. The system bound a diverse elite, including Hindu Rajput princes, to the imperial state.

title: Prince Shōtoku's Seventeen Articles
body: Traditionally dated to 604, this Japanese text attributed to Prince Shōtoku sets out moral principles for officials, beginning with the value of harmony. Drawing on Confucian and Buddhist ideas, it urges consultation on important matters and loyalty to the sovereign. Its authorship is debated and it is not a constitution in the modern sense, but it is a founding text of Japanese political thought.

title: The Seneca Falls Convention
body: In July 1848 Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Lucretia Mott and others held the first women's rights convention in the United States at Seneca Falls, New York. Its Declaration of Sentiments, modelled on the Declaration of Independence, listed grievances against men's domination and demanded, among other things, women's right to vote. It is seen as the start of the organised American women's movement.

title: Poland's Solidarity Movement
body: Founded in 1980 after strikes at the Gdańsk shipyard led by Lech Wałęsa, Solidarity was the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc and soon had around ten million members. Banned under martial law in 1981, it returned to negotiate with the communist government in 1989, winning partly free elections that helped bring down communism across Eastern Europe.

title: Realism in International Relations
body: Realism holds that states, lacking any world government above them, pursue power and security in an anarchic international system. Its roots are traced to Thucydides' account of the Peloponnesian War, Machiavelli and Hobbes, and it was developed in the 20th century by Hans Morgenthau and Kenneth Waltz. Its main rival, liberalism, stresses institutions, trade and cooperation.

title: Apartheid
body: From 1948 South Africa's National Party government built a system of racial segregation, classifying people by race and controlling where they could live, work, marry and vote. Resistance by the African National Congress and others, together with international sanctions, led to negotiations in the early 1990s. The first elections open to all races, in 1994, made Nelson Mandela president.

title: The Constitution of Medina
body: Soon after Muhammad's migration to Medina in 622, an agreement was drawn up defining the community formed by Muslims, Jewish tribes and others in the city, with mutual obligations and ways of settling disputes. Known only through later sources, its exact date and wording are debated. It is often cited as an early written compact governing a plural community.

title: Brown v. Board of Education
body: In 1954 the US Supreme Court unanimously ruled that racial segregation in public schools violated the Constitution's guarantee of equal protection, holding that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal. It rejected the 'separate but equal' doctrine of Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) and became a catalyst for the civil rights movement.
